blocks.text: 1. Hybrid Retrieval

blocks.alt: Graph traversal combines with vector search

blocks.text: Cypher Queries closed by noting that different graph databases support different query languages while the underlying concept stays the same. Hybrid Retrieval, combining graph traversal with vector similarity search in one pipeline, closes out this Graph RAG module by bringing graph retrieval back together with the vector methods covered throughout the rest of this course.
It runs both retrieval methods and merges their results rather than choosing only one.
2. Neither Method Covers Everything

blocks.alt: Graph only is compared against vector only

blocks.text: As covered generally in Graph RAG, graph traversal finds precise, explicit relationship chains but misses loosely related prose.
Vector search finds loosely related prose but misses precise relationship chains.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","What it misses"],"rows":[["Graph traversal","Loosely related prose without explicit relationships"],["Vector search","Precise, explicit relationship chains"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Routing Decides Which Method To Use

blocks.alt: A query goes through a router to decide graph or vector

blocks.text: As with routing between retrieval strategies in Dynamic Routing, a query recognizably needing a relationship chain can route to graph traversal specifically.
A loosely worded question can route to vector search instead.
4. Running Both And Merging Results

blocks.alt: Graph results and vector results merge together

blocks.text: As with reciprocal rank fusion merging results in Fusion RAG, rather than choosing only one method, hybrid retrieval can run both and merge their separate result lists.
It is the same rank based merging technique, applied here across two very different retrieval methods.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Reciprocal rank fusion does not care what produced each ranked list, so it merges a graph traversal result list and a vector search result list exactly the same way it merges two vector search lists.

blocks.text: 5. Graph Results Enrich Vector Retrieved Chunks

blocks.alt: A vector-retrieved chunk gets enriched with graph context

blocks.text: A vector retrieved chunk can be enriched with the specific graph facts about the entities it mentions.
This combines the passage's narrative context with the graph's precise, structured facts.
6. Vector Search Can Identify The Starting Entity

blocks.alt: Vector search identifies a starting entity for graph traversal

blocks.text: As with starting from a known entity in Graph Traversal, a vector search over entity descriptions can identify which node a traversal should actually start from.
The two methods can feed into each other, not just run side by side.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A vague query mentioning a company by a loose description rather than its exact name can be resolved to a starting node through vector search over entity descriptions, before graph traversal even begins.

blocks.text: 7. Hybrid Pipelines Add Real Complexity
As with each added step costing latency in Advanced RAG, maintaining both a graph database and a vector index doubles the infrastructure to build and keep current.
It is a real operational cost beyond running either system alone.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Setup","Infrastructure to maintain"],"rows":[["Vector search alone","One vector index"],["Hybrid retrieval","Both a graph database and a vector index"]]}

blocks.text: 8. When One Is Enough On Its Own

As with recognizing when a knowledge graph is the right structure for the data in Knowledge Graphs, not every knowledge base actually has both rich relationships and loosely related prose worth combining.
Hybrid retrieval only pays off when both signals exist in the data.
9. Recognizing When Hybrid Retrieval Earns Its Combined Infrastructure Cost

blocks.alt: Needing both structure and semantics points toward hybrid retrieval

blocks.text: Data with both rich relationships and loosely related prose benefits from combining both methods.
Data suited to only one retrieval style, by contrast, does not need the added hybrid complexity.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Choosing only one retrieval method when the data actually has both signals worth combining.
Running both graph and vector retrieval for every query even when a router could pick one.
Missing the opportunity to let vector search resolve a graph traversal's starting entity.
Adding hybrid retrieval infrastructure to a knowledge base that only ever needs one method.

blocks.text: 12. Graph RAG: Module Complete

items: Knowledge Graphs: structured networks of entities and the relationships connecting them.
Entity Extraction: identifying individual entities mentioned in raw source text.
Relation Extraction: identifying how already extracted entities connect to each other.
Graph Construction: assembling extracted entities and relations into one queryable graph.
Graph Traversal: walking the constructed graph outward from a starting entity to find an answer.
Cypher Queries: the concrete, declarative query language most graph databases use to express traversal.
Hybrid Retrieval: combining graph traversal with vector similarity search in one pipeline.
Graph traversal finds precise relationship chains; vector search finds loosely related prose.
The two methods can feed into each other, not just run side by side and merge afterward.
This closes the Graph RAG module; the Evaluation module covers measuring RAG system quality next.
